rationale: The official PMC HTML contains 216 numbered titles and also carries withdrawal notices. Member 27 measures patient and caregiver knowledge. Member 222 describes a six-person sham comparison in dementia with Lewy bodies and separately cites the earlier Parkinson dementia stimulation trial. Member 225 reports one new visual hallucination after subthalamic surgery among 36 Parkinson participants. Members 22 and 23 concern pantothenate-kinase-associated neurodegeneration. These outcomes use no dried fig ingestion comparison.

Investigators compared 33 dementia-with-Lewy-bodies patients, 18 posterior cortical atrophy patients and 100 cognitively unimpaired controls. Clinical assessment identified visual hallucinations in 13 of the Lewy body group and two of the atrophy group. The PET contrast concerns tracer uptake and syndrome differentiation. The clinical counts describe symptom presence.

The review summarizes the phenotype, biology, diagnosis and treatments of dementia with Lewy bodies. Visual hallucinations are a clinical feature and are discussed across earlier sources. The review gives no dried fig exposure comparison.

This review examines diabetes-related and other treatment pathways, trial literature, and cognition in Parkinson disease. Neuropsychiatric symptoms provide clinical and medication context, with no dried fig or food-timed visual episode contrast.

The article covers novel assessment technologies and treatment applications in Parkinson disease, including imaging, modeling and monitoring. Hallucinations are mentioned in describing the condition. No dietary fig exposure or visual hallucination event rate is reported.

One hundred neurologists and 100 psychiatrists were surveyed about evaluation and treatment. Possible aggravation of visual hallucinations was frequently given as a reason to avoid increasing levodopa. The response measures reported clinical practice and concern rather than monitored visual events following food.

Seventy-two patients with diverse entry diagnoses ultimately had established dementia with Lewy bodies. Cases were compared by blinded PET classification and follow-up diagnosis. Relatives sometimes reported visual symptoms without psychometric confirmation at entry. The visual symptom fractions record diagnostic presence by group, without an exposure-linked event measure.

The article reviews resting-state imaging and network methods across parkinsonian syndromes. The clinical symptom literature includes hallucinations. Imaging and clinical distinctions provide phenotype context without a dried fig comparison.

The study compares metabolic patterns and clinical measures, including olfaction and executive function, across sleep and Parkinson groups and controls. These outcomes do not measure visual episodes after fig consumption.

The sample includes 57 patients with dementia with Lewy bodies, 32 people with Parkinson disease without dementia and 56 controls. The comparison addresses blood protein signatures and diagnostic group differences. It does not measure fig intake or repeated visual episodes.

Of 107 patients prescribed pimavanserin for Parkinson-related psychosis, 91 began treatment. The charts recorded clinical psychosis improvement for 69 of 91. The endpoint combines forms of psychosis, including delusions and different hallucination modalities. The uncontrolled drug review supplies no estimate for the isolated visual episode rate after food.

Probable Lewy body dementia, Alzheimer disease and control participants supplied resting EEG data. The primary analysis focuses on dynamics and cognitive fluctuations. Visual hallucinations are part of characterized disease presentation, and the comparison does not test dried fig intake.

The study recruited 102 older participants from two independent contemporary samples and used an analyzed cohort after exclusions. The authors report no clear association of selected dynamic connectivity measures with visual hallucination severity in dementia with Lewy bodies. The outcome is an imaging correlation with symptoms rather than a food intervention.

Twenty-nine Parkinson participants and eight controls were examined for links between hippocampal subfield measures and episodic memory. Cognitive and structural endpoints are distinct from waking visual episodes after food.

This methods paper assesses hesitation and step detection in older people navigating routes of different complexity, including people with Alzheimer disease. The walking task and signal-classification outcomes do not measure hallucinations in Parkinson disease after a dietary exposure.

The review compiles disease mechanisms and overlapping Lewy pathology in Alzheimer disease, including clinical hallucination context. It contains no original dried fig exposure or timed visual outcome comparison.

The article compares structural imaging correlates of hallucination status across diagnostic categories. It distinguishes mechanisms, modalities and clinical samples. The component comparisons characterize hallucinatory status rather than measuring a dietary fig intervention.
The article summarizes gene associations and pathogenic mechanisms in Parkinson disease. Clinical phenotype descriptions provide context rather than an estimate of visual episodes after dried figs.

The paper discusses sleep changes, REM sleep behavior disorder and clinical progression. Its sleep phenotypes and clinical symptom references do not measure visual hallucination frequency after a named food.
The article relates an observed imaging marker to neuropathology in dementia with Lewy bodies, including clinical phenotype. No dried fig comparison or dietary event count appears.

The review tracks deep brain stimulation outcomes across inherited Parkinson genes. The treatments and comparisons are surgical and stimulation related. Clinical adverse features do not establish a food effect.

The review distinguishes sleep disorders and associated clinical manifestations across autoimmune neurological conditions. Disease and symptom context differ from an edible fig and Parkinson visual rate comparison.

The authors discuss simple visual illusions, formed hallucinations, bodily symptoms and neurological circuit models in Parkinson disease and dementia with Lewy bodies. The clinical and imaging literature provides mechanistic context without an original fig intake comparison.

The case documents perceptual disturbances in an acute presentation and considers medication context and diagnosis. The symptoms and clinical trajectory supply no dried fig exposure timing or event rate.

The paper reviews neuropsychiatric syndromes across neurodegenerative diseases and summarizes drug and supportive-treatment evidence. Visual hallucinations appear in disease and treatment discussions. A dried fig comparison is absent.

MRI compares hippocampal measures in 14 dementia-with-Lewy-bodies patients and 62 people with Parkinson disease. The regional structure outcome does not estimate visual hallucination frequency after a culinary exposure.

The review synthesizes diagnostic guidance and clinical distinctions in young-onset dementia. Hallucinations can inform differential diagnosis. Expert guidance and supporting studies do not supply evidence for dried fig intake.

The study examines an alpha-synuclein RT-QuIC assay in patient and control CSF. The measured result is assay discrimination, while clinical features characterize disease. There is no food consumption and visual episode comparison.

The SPIN cohort records clinical testing, imaging and biospecimen collection for neurodegenerative biomarker validation. The cohort description and clinical ascertainment do not measure a specific dietary fig effect.

The chapter describes clinical neuroimaging across aging and multiple neurologic disorders. Its disease examples and diagnostic patterns do not establish a timed visual outcome following dried fig intake.

The survey relates skin color and hair redness to self-reported physical and mental health items, including perceptual complaints. It does not use a food intervention, assign a Parkinson-specific visual outcome or measure dried fig consumption.

Investigators compared visual evoked potentials in 29 women with self-reported migraine and 31 healthy comparison participants. Perceptual symptom discussion and cortical responses concern migraine, with no ingestion-linked Parkinson visual outcomes.

A case of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease presented with rapidly progressive parkinsonism and visual symptoms. The diagnosis and neurological course are differential-diagnosis context and give no dried fig exposure or separate visual event count.

Parkinson participants and study partners rated the impact of cognition on instrumental activities of daily living. Subjective and partner reports and neuropsychological measures address function. The study does not record visual episode rates after a food intervention.

The review discusses applications of wireless and mobile EEG to cognitive impairment across settings. EEG and cognition outcomes, and mentions of disease features, do not supply a dried fig exposure contrast.
